post.caption: Girandole earrings share a name with fireworks. It comes from Italian girandola, tied to a verb meaning to turn. In English it first meant a firework in the 1600s. The same word also names a branched candlestick. The earrings are named after that candlestick. The classic design is a bow with three pear shaped drops. They were a leading earring style of the 1700s. Some were made in glass paste instead of gems. Heavy pairs could be tied to the hair with a ribbon. When the style faded, many pairs were taken apart and reused. A Paris pattern book from 1770 showed girandole designs.
